title: Call orchestration, resilient streaming semantics, and SDK ergonomics - PRD (draft)
content:
Summary:
This PRD proposes a unified approach to call orchestration for the Hosted API that addresses three developer pain points at once: predictable streaming semantics under partial failures, explicit tool-calling contracts for composability, and ergonomic SDK surface patterns that make the above easy to adopt. The goal is to ship an initial beta that enables teams to compose model calls with deterministic envelopes, client-side fallback hooks, and minimal SDK friction so that product teams can safely roll streaming + tool-call features into production.

Problem statement / motivation:
- Current streaming behaviour is inconsistent across SDKs and language runtimes: partial responses (mid-stream disconnects, backend fallbacks) surface as raw text fragments to clients with no structured signal about intent/failure.
- Tool calls (external function invocation patterns) are brittle when tools fail, when models return ambiguous tool payloads, or when schema evolves. Teams end up building ad-hoc glue logic and complex retry semantics in-app.
- SDKs prioritize simple textual streaming but lack small composability primitives (interceptors, typed adapters, local emulation) to make tool-calling and structured output ergonomic and debuggable.

Value hypothesis / success metrics:
- Developer adoption: 30% of new Hosted API integrations within 3 months use the orchestration SDK primitives or structured envelopes.
- Error surface clarity: reduce customer-reported incidents rooted in ambiguous partial-streams by 50% in first quarter post-launch (tracked via support tags and Postgres incidents).
- Latency/SLO: median first-token latency unaffected (<5% regression) and 95th percentile end-to-end generation latency within current SLOs for target models.
- Business metric: reduction in average engineering time to integrate tool-calling from 2 weeks -> 3 days (anecdotally measured through customer interviews and solutions-eng intake).

User personas and primary journeys:
- Frontend engineer (chat UI): needs predictable stream events to render partial responses and UI affordances such as tool-call prompts, progress bars, and graceful error banners.
- Backend integration engineer (workflow orchestrator): needs typed tool-call results, clear failure reasons, and simple retry/fallback hooks without building a custom orchestration layer.
- SDK consumer (data-processing job): wants lightweight local emulation for tests and replay to enable deterministic CI.

Design principles / constraints:
- Backwards compatible: existing non-structured streaming clients should continue to work by default. Structured envelopes should be opt-in.
- Minimal surface area: SDKs provide small primitives (envelopes, interceptors, adapters) rather than monolithic frameworks.
- Explicit failure states: every stream/frame includes an envelope with an explicit kind/tag (content, tool-call, checkpoint, error, final).
- Observability: traceable request IDs and per-frame telemetry to Console for debugging rollouts.

Proposed API and runtime semantics (high-level):
1) Enveloped streaming frames
- Every chunked/frameed stream returns JSON-lines envelopes alongside free-text frames. Envelope fields (string keys): kind, request_id, seq, partial (true|false), payload_type, payload (string or JSON).
- kind values: content, tool_call, checkpoint, fallback_notice, error, final.
- SDKs expose a streaming iterator that yields typed events (ContentEvent, ToolCallEvent, CheckpointEvent, ErrorEvent, FinalEvent). Raw text mode flattens ContentEvent.payload into the old string stream for backwards compat.

2) Tool-call contract and schema evolution
- ToolCallEvent contains: tool_name, version_tag, args (stringified JSON), suggested_retry (none|idempotent|safe-retry), correlation_hint.
- Tools register with a compact schema registry (managed by platform) that returns a lightweight json-schema-like descriptor. SDKs validate incoming tool payloads and surface structured errors when mismatch occurs.
- When tool schema evolves, runtime returns version_tag and a deprecation_hint. Clients can request a best-effort compatibility mode (server attempts to translate if possible).

3) Resiliency and fallback semantics
- Partial failure (e.g., worker preemption) emits a fallback_notice envelope describing fallback model variant or degraded mode. SDKs call user-provided on_fallback(callback) hooks that can decide: continue, switch-to-local, call-alternate-tool, abort-with-value.
- CheckpointEvent signals safe replay points. SDKs expose checkpoint-aware retry: client can instruct the platform to resume from a checkpoint (idempotent resume) rather than restarting whole conversation.

4) SDK ergonomics and surface patterns
- Fluent builder for request construction with typed tool adapters. Example: client.request().withModel("redwood-1-7b").withTool(toolDef).withStreaming().send();
- Interceptors: small middleware hooks (pre-send, on-frame, on-final) for logging, metrics, transformation. Interceptors compose and are chainable.
- Local emulator: a lightweight node/py process that can mimic envelope streams (deterministic fixtures) for CI and offline testing. Emulation supports injecting error frames and checkpoint jumps.
- Minimal code example (pseudo):
  const client = Redwood.hostedClient();
  client.addInterceptor(loggerInterceptor);
  const stream = await client.stream({model: 'rwd-1', tools:['calendar-v1']});
  for await (const evt of stream) {
    if (evt.kind === 'tool_call') {
      const res = myCalendar.call(evt.payload);
      stream.sendToolResult(evt.request_id, res);
    }
  }

Non-goals:
- Full orchestration runtime (we are not building a stateful orchestration engine or workflow language; clients remain responsible for complex business logic).
- Replacing customer-owned schema registries; we provide lightweight descriptors to make tool-calling safe but not a full enterprise schema service.

Security & compliance:
- Tool payloads marked sensitive will be redacted in Console logs by default; SDKs surface a redaction flag on events.
- All tool-call artifacts are subject to tenant isolation and existing audit-log hooks.

Observability / telemetry:
- New telemetry events at frame-level: frame_kind, latency_since_request, cumulative_tokens, worker_variant, tool_name.
- Console will show stream play-by-play with checkpoint markers and fallback notices.

Rollout plan and milestones (quarterly):
- Phase 0 (2 weeks): API Spec finalization, envelope wire format, and SDK contract review.
- Phase 1 (6 weeks): Server runtime support for envelopes + fallback_notice and checkpoint; Node SDK prototype.
- Phase 2 (4 weeks): Python SDK parity, local emulator alpha, Console stream view for play-by-play.
- Phase 3 (6 weeks): Beta with opt-in flag for a set of beta customers, gather feedback, iterate on schema registry integration and tool-versioning UX.
- Phase 4 (ongoing): Gradual opt-out migration path and public docs / examples.

Open questions / risks:
- Wire format size overhead: JSON-line envelopes increase token payloads — measure impact and consider binary compact encoding (msgpack/protobuf) for high-throughput customers.
- Backwards compatibility edge cases where older clients interpret envelopes as text — need robust header negotiation.
- Policy around ambiguous tool outputs: when model returns both free text and tool_call in same frame, which takes precedence? Proposed: explicit priority rules documented and enforced server-side.

Telemetry dashboards / KPIs to build before beta:
- Per-request frame breakdown distribution (percent content vs tool_call vs error).
- Frequency and causes of fallback_notice frames.
- Average number of checkpoint resumes per request (indicates usage of resume API).

Dependencies / cross-team touches:
- Serving-runtime: envelope framing and checkpoint resume hooks.
- Developer-experience: SDK ergonomics and local emulator.
- Console/observability: stream play-by-play UI and redaction rules.
- Solutions-engineering: onboarding beta customers and writing integration recipes.

Next steps (this doc):
- Align on envelope schema in a short working session with serving-runtime and devx (week of 2026-03-15).
- Build Node SDK prototype and 2 integration recipes (chat + calendar tool-call) for the beta cohort.
- Create a lightweight compatibility test-suite to run against existing non-structured clients to ensure no regressions.

Appendix: short examples and failure scenarios
- Scenario A: Worker preemption mid-stream -> server emits fallback_notice (variant: smaller model) + checkpoint id -> SDK on_fallback receives notice and decides to show a UI banner while continuing the stream.
- Scenario B: Model issues tool_call with args that don't validate -> ToolCallEvent includes validation_error (schema_mismatch) and suggested_retry=none; SDK surfaces a structured error object so client can prompt user to supply corrected args.
- Scenario C: Checkpoint resume for long-running job -> client resumes from checkpoint id to avoid replaying entire context, saving tokens/cost.

This document is intentionally prescriptive on envelopes and SDK primitives while keeping the orchestration logic minimal and client-driven. Feedback requested: preferred envelope field names, tradeoffs on compact vs human-readable encoding, and SDK ergonomic patterns we should prototype first (interceptors vs reactive streams vs callbacks).
